text: Sweden spent years building a giant warship. It sailed for about twenty minutes.
It had sixty-four guns and hundreds of painted sculptures.
The King had approved the design himself.
But before it sailed, they tested it.
About thirty men ran back and forth across the deck.
The ship rocked so hard, they feared it would tip over at the dock.
So they stopped the test.
And they sent it out anyway.
On August tenth, sixteen twenty-eight, it set sail with a cannon salute.
There was only a light breeze.
Then one strong gust hit.
The ship leaned, and water poured in through its open cannon hatches.
It sank in the harbour, and at least thirty people died.
You see, a ship is like a punching-bag toy. Its weight sits low, so it rolls back up.
But the Vasa had heavy guns stacked high, so it was top-heavy.
One gust was enough to tip it over.
There was an inquiry. Who was to blame?
Officially, nobody.
The blame quietly landed on the shipbuilder, who had died the year before.
In nineteen sixty-one, the Vasa was raised. Today it is ninety-eight percent original.
As a warship, it lasted about twenty minutes. As a museum, it has been packed for over thirty years.
